status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: IMMIG items are about policy; NATION items are about what membership in the nation means. The pilot tests whether these are one axis or two.

items.stem: About 1 million people get permanent legal residence (green cards) each year. What should that number be?
items.scope: Permanent legal immigration only, not temporary visas or refugees.
options: 2 million or more
About 1.5 million
About 1 million, as now
About 500,000
Fewer than 250,000

facts.claim: Roughly 1.0-1.2 million lawful permanent residents admitted per year in recent fiscal years
facts.source: DHS Office of Homeland Security Statistics, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics

items.stem: Should the US admit more or fewer temporary foreign workers for seasonal farm and service jobs?
items.scope: Workers who come on visas for a season or a few years, then return home.
options: Many more than today
Somewhat more
About the same
Somewhat fewer
Many fewer

items.stem: Should the US admit more or fewer temporary foreign workers for skilled jobs, such as engineers and programmers?
items.scope: Workers who come on visas for a set number of years.
options: Many more than today
Somewhat more
About the same
Somewhat fewer
Many fewer
items.notes: Split from temp_workers in review: views on skilled and seasonal visas differ, including within parties.

items.stem: How should the US mainly choose who gets green cards?
items.scope: Today about two-thirds are based on family ties to people already here.
options: Mostly family ties, as now
An even mix of family ties and job skills
Mostly job skills and education, as in Canada and Australia

facts.claim: Family-sponsored and immediate-relative categories account for roughly 60-65% of new green cards

items.stem: Which relatives should US citizens be able to sponsor to immigrate?
items.scope: Sponsoring means the relative can apply for a green card through the citizen.
options: Spouses, children, parents and siblings, with shorter waits than today
Spouses, children, parents and siblings, as today
Only spouses, minor children and parents
Only spouses and minor children

items.stem: Which comes closest to how the US should handle the southern border?
items.scope: Think about the border with Mexico.
options: Fewer agents and barriers than today
Keep about current enforcement
More agents and technology, but no new physical wall
A wall along most of the border, plus more agents

items.stem: Should the military be used to stop people from crossing the border without permission?
items.scope: US troops stationed at the southern border.
options: No; border control should be left to civilian agencies
Troops can support border agents with transport and surveillance, but not stop people
Yes, troops should stop people and turn them back

items.stem: Should all employers be required to check electronically that new hires are allowed to work in the US?
items.scope: Using a federal online system called E-Verify.
options: No; it burdens workers and businesses
Only large employers
Yes, all employers, with heavy fines for hiring people without legal status

items.stem: Should local police help federal immigration agents find and detain people living here without legal status?
items.scope: Local police and jails in your state, under any administration.
options: No; local police should not help at all
Only for people convicted of serious crimes
Yes, whenever federal agents ask

items.stem: People fleeing persecution can ask for asylum in the US. Which comes closest to your view?
items.scope: Think of people arriving at the southern border.
options: Make it easier to apply, and let applicants live and work here while they wait
Keep the right to apply here, but decide cases much faster
Require people to apply from outside the US or in the first safe country they reach
End or sharply limit asylum at the southern border

definitions.text: Protection for people already in or arriving at the US who fear persecution in their home country because of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a social group.

items.stem: Should people fleeing gang violence or domestic abuse in their home country qualify for asylum?
items.scope: People whose own government is not the one threatening them.
options: Yes, whether or not their own government could protect them
Only if their own government can't or won't protect them
No; asylum should be only for people targeted for their race, religion, politics or similar reasons

items.stem: How many refugees should the US resettle each year?
items.scope: Refugees are screened abroad before they come, unlike asylum seekers.
items.context: Since 1980 the yearly limit has ranged from under 10,000 to over 200,000.
options: 125,000 or more
Fewer than 10,000
None

facts.claim: Refugee ceilings range from 7,500 (FY2026, record low) to 231,700 (FY1980)
facts.source: Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for FY2026 (Oct 2025); State Department Refugee Processing Center
facts.note: FY1980 figure from historical ceilings table; spot-check.

items.stem: Should children born in the US automatically be citizens?
items.scope: Children born on US soil, whatever their parents' situation.
options: Yes, all children born here
Only if at least one parent is a citizen or has legal permanent residence
Only if at least one parent is a citizen

items.stem: How much should immigrants be expected to adopt American customs and ways of life?
items.scope: Think of immigrants who plan to stay permanently.
options: Not at all; they should keep their own customs if they wish
Learn English and follow the law, but keep their own culture freely
Learn English and adopt most American customs
Fully blend in and leave their old customs behind

items.stem: How important is each of these to being truly American?
items.scope: Answer each one separately.
options: Not important
Somewhat important
Very important

cases.text: Having family in the US for several generations

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of what makes someone American?
items.scope: This is about belonging, not legal citizenship.
options: Believing in the country's ideals, like freedom and equality; anyone can become American
Those ideals plus learning English and sharing the culture
Being born here or raised in the culture from childhood

items.stem: Overall, how should public schools teach American history?
items.scope: Middle and high school history classes.
options: Give the country's failures and injustices at least as much attention as its achievements
Teach failures and achievements in balance
Emphasize achievements and ideals so students take pride in the country

items.stem: Is kneeling during the national anthem an acceptable way to protest?
items.scope: For example, by athletes before a game, for any cause.
options: Yes, always acceptable
Acceptable, but not at official government or military events
Not acceptable; it disrespects the country

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Think about the country as a whole over the long run.

sides.label: Many cultures
sides.text: America is stronger when groups keep their own cultures, even if people share less in common.

sides.label: One shared culture
sides.text: America is stronger when people adopt one shared culture, even if some traditions fade.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.stem: Should US citizens be allowed to also be citizens of another country?
items.scope: Today this is allowed.
options: Yes, as today
Yes, except for people in high government office
No; citizens should hold only US citizenship

items.stem: Compared with other countries, which comes closest to your view of the US?
items.scope: Think about the country overall, not its current government.
options: Many countries are better
It's no better or worse than many other countries
It's one of the greatest countries, along with some others
It stands above all other countries

items.stem: Should English be the official language of the US, with government business done only in English?
items.scope: Federal, state and local government services and documents.
options: No; government should offer services in many languages
Official language, but keep things like ballots and health information in other languages
Yes, English only for government business

items.subtopic: Citizens first for jobs and benefits
items.stem: Should US citizens get preference over legal immigrants for jobs and government benefits?
items.scope: Legal permanent residents, not people without legal status.
options: No; legal immigrants should be treated the same
Only for government jobs
Yes, for government jobs and benefits
Yes, and private employers should have to show no citizen is available before hiring a non-citizen

items.subtopic: Immigrant selection by culture or religion
items.stem: Should the US consider an immigrant's culture or religion when deciding who may come?
items.scope: Legal immigration, after security screening.
options: No; culture and religion should never count
Only knowledge of English and US civics should count
Give some preference to people from countries with cultures closer to America's
Yes, and bar people from some religions or cultures

items.stem: When enforcing immigration law against people without legal status, should agents be allowed to do each of these?
items.scope: Answer each case separately.
options: Should not be allowed
Should be allowed

cases.text: Make arrests at places of worship
Hold families with children in detention
Deport people to a country that isn't their own
Wear masks to hide their identity while working
